summary: Cast-iron caisson light on Plum Beach Shoal in Narragansett Bay: first permanent light 1899, dark 1941, relit 2003 by a nonprofit that owns it.

access.note: Tower closed to visitors. Best seen from the water, from the Jamestown bridge or from the shore at either end of the bridge.

facts.agency: Friends of Plum Beach Lighthouse, Inc. (nonprofit; owns the tower)

events.note: Temporary red lantern on the unfinished foundation, 1 February 1897
1,028-pound fog bell struck by machinery, 1 June 1897
Fourth-order light, flashing white every 5 seconds, first shown 1 July 1899
Temporary lens apparatus from depot stock, which the Board wanted replaced (estimate $857)
Winter ice cracked the tower (LighthouseFriends); the nomination dates the ice damage to spring 1919
Crack repairs and riprap at the foundation completed
1938 hurricane: the keepers on duty rode it out in the tower
Unmanned and automated after the 1938 hurricane
Deactivated 1 May 1941, after the Jamestown bridge made it unnecessary
A private company proposed moving the tower to a condominium complex in Quincy, Massachusetts; the Friends were formed to keep it in place
State of Rhode Island gave the tower to the Friends of Plum Beach Lighthouse
Exterior restored; over 50 tons of droppings removed
Relit in December 2003 with a solar-powered beacon flashing white every five seconds
New rotating LED beacon, funded by a local charitable trust

corrections.why: 1897 was a temporary red lantern on the unfinished foundation (Board, 1896-97). The permanent fourth-order light was first shown 1 July 1899 (Board, 1900; LighthouseFriends).
Tower completed May 1899 (Board, 1899); the nomination gives the tower's build date as 1899; work began in 1896.
The light was shown in 1899 and deactivated in 1941; 2003 was a relighting by the Friends with a solar beacon.

corrections.proposed: 1999 transferred to the Friends of Plum Beach Lighthouse
corrections.why: The tower was not deactivated in 1999; it was deactivated in 1941 and the state transferred title to the Friends in 1999.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Board's report gives $20,000 under the act of 2 March 1895; the NRHP nomination gives $10,000; LighthouseFriends gives $20,000 in 1895 and $40,000 in 1896. The story uses the Board's figure.
The record's 1897 is the start of work and a temporary light shown 1 February 1897. The tower was completed in May 1899 and the permanent fourth-order light was first shown 1 July 1899.

The nomination says the rock pile was laid after the spring 1919 ice. The Board recorded 1,500 tons placed in February 1897; the Lighthouse Service bulletins show 1920 bids rejected and 1922 completion; LighthouseFriends adds 9,000 tons in 1922. The later work appears to be a second riprap campaign after the ice, on top of the 1897 pile.
LighthouseFriends says the bridge opened in 1940; the nomination says 1941. Both give 1 May 1941 for deactivation of the light.

The Board's 1899 report calls the lens then in use a temporary apparatus; the USLHS record and a local history site describe a fourth-order Fresnel lens; the nomination says the lamp and lens "have been removed" (undated). The sources do not give a date for the permanent lens.
LighthouseFriends gives waves as high as 35 feet; a local history site gives a 30-foot wave. Both are cited; the story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Not checked against a primary keeper register beyond the USLHS roster (NARA-derived). Sources disagree on the 1895 appropriation, the riprap history, the bridge opening year and the 1938 wave height; the story gives the disagreement. The Rhode Island history site says Judson G. Allen was a witness in a 1916 liquor-licence trial and resigned after a Board inquiry; the USLHS roster has Allen at Plum Beach only 1899-1904, so the claim is unverified and left out. The Friends' history calls John Ganze 'the keeper' in 1938; the roster and LighthouseFriends make him first assistant (the story follows the roster). Edwin Babcock is named by LighthouseFriends, the Friends and the Rhode Island site but is not on the USLHS roster; his line has no person id. The USLHS roster prints 'George Doig (Doige)' and the record's 'built 1897' and 'first_lit 1897' describe the start of work; see corrections. The record lists a 2003 first_lit; the sources describe a relighting. The current lens is not described in the sources read; the 2025 rotating LED beacon is the current optic per LighthouseFriends. Access: the tower is closed and reached by water; no landing is described for the public. The USLHS place page's coordinates (41.5248, -71.4033) differ from the record by about 0.6 km; the record's OSM position is consistent with LighthouseFriends and ARLHS and was left unchanged. Verification pass 2026-10-22: the 1938 accounts differ. LighthouseFriends says Babcock and Ganze could not leave before the storm; the Friends' history says Babcock had been visiting Ganze, tried to row back to shore and returned. Both are stated in the story. The Friends also call Ganze 'the keeper at the time' where the roster and LighthouseFriends make him first assistant. The Friends date the start of construction to 1897; the Board's report and LighthouseFriends give work from July 1896, and the story uses 1896. Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1938 p. 39 is OCR'd in two interleaved columns: the story keeps only the words that read in sequence ('assistant keeper, Walter B. Eberle', 'person at the station at the time', 'lost his life') and drops 'first', which is not contiguous in the OCR. The 1899 Board report's OCR reads 'surmonnted' and 'saperstracture'; the story corrects the spelling in its quotation and the evidence keeps the OCR. The 1893, 1895, 1896-97, 1899 and 1900 Board pages were checked against the Internet Archive page index (scan pages 78, 246, 312, 104 and 15). The 1891-92 page (scan 403) matches the quotation. The USLHS roster lists 23 first-assistant lines, one name twice for 1910; the story says so.
